speaker: John Schulman
title: John Schulman (OpenAI Cofounder) — Reasoning, RLHF, & plan for 2027 AGI
question: In frontier AI development, how durable of a competitive moat is superior post-training?
guest: I think there's something of a moat because it's just a very complex operation. You have to have a lot of skilled people doing it, so there's a lot of tacit knowledge and organizational knowledge that's required. Creating a model that actually has all the functionality people care about requires an accumulation of a lot of R&D, so it's not trivial to spin this up immediately. It does seem like the same companies putting together the most serious pre-training efforts are also putting together serious post-training efforts, so it is somewhat possible to copy or spin up more of these efforts. There's also one force that makes it less of a moat: you can distill the models, take someone else's model and clone the outputs, or use someone else's model as a judge to do comparisons. The bigger players probably aren't doing that because it goes against terms of service policies and would be a hit to their pride, but I would expect some of the smaller players are doing that to get off the ground. And that catches you up to a large extent.

points.core: Post-training creates a real operational moat through accumulated tacit organizational knowledge.
points.note: Accept: hard-to-replicate institutional know-how, accumulated R&D, or complex operational pipelines run by skilled teams that cannot be spun up overnight. Do not credit: claiming post-training is only about proprietary datasets or compute.

points.core: Distilling a rival model's outputs rapidly erodes the post-training moat.
points.note: Accept: cloning outputs from a frontier model or training on competitor generations to catch up quickly. Do not credit: generic claims that open-source papers leak algorithms.

points.core: Using a frontier model as an evaluation judge accelerates catching up.
points.note: Accept: using a stronger competitor model as a reward judge or pairwise evaluator to bootstrap post-training. Do not credit: merely mentioning synthetic data without referencing competitor-as-judge or output cloning.

points.core: Major frontier labs avoid competitor distillation because of terms-of-service restrictions.
points.note: Accept: top labs refraining from distilling rivals due to ToS policies, legal/policy constraints, or institutional pride, leaving smaller players to exploit it. Do not credit: claiming distillation is technically impossible for large labs.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Not very durable on its own; it is best thought of as a lead measured in months, not years.

Post-training (fine-tuning, RLHF, reinforcement learning on tasks, character and tool-use shaping) clearly matters. It accounts for much of the difference users feel between models built on comparable pretraining, especially in coding, agentic reliability and personality.

But the techniques themselves diffuse quickly. Researchers move between labs, methods get published or reverse-engineered, and competitors can distil from a rival's outputs. Historically, any behavioural edge one lab ships has been roughly matched by others within one or two release cycles.

What is more durable is the machinery behind post-training rather than any particular recipe: proprietary usage data and feedback loops, hard-to-build RL environments and evaluations, expert human data pipelines, and the accumulated tacit judgment or "taste" about what good model behaviour looks like. These compound with scale and distribution, and are harder to copy than an algorithm.

So superior post-training is a real but leaky advantage. It becomes a moat only when coupled with data flywheels, compute and organisational execution that keep regenerating the lead.

points.why: The response identifies accumulated tacit judgment and expert-run pipelines as durable, hard-to-copy operational advantages.
quotes: expert human data pipelines, and the accumulated tacit judgment or "taste" about what good model behaviour looks like.
These compound with scale and distribution, and are harder to copy than an algorithm.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Superior post-training provides a meaningful short-term lead—typically lasting months rather than years—making it an operational edge rather than a durable standalone moat. Because post-training governs how a model reasons, follows instructions, uses tools, and feels to users, excellence here drives immediate product differentiation and adoption. Yet purely algorithmic gains erode quickly. Techniques like reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards and preference tuning diffuse rapidly through talent mobility, while distillation lets rivals extract behavioral polish and reasoning patterns from leading outputs at low cost. 

Post-training becomes defensible only when backed by proprietary assets that outsiders cannot easily replicate: real-world user feedback flywheels, bespoke execution environments for training long-horizon agents, and scarce domain-expert verifiers in fields like coding or science. Even then, post-training remains bounded by base-model capacity. Ultimately, superior post-training acts less like a permanent fortress and more like a treadmill—essential for turning raw compute into reliable products, yet durable only alongside frontier pre-training scale and entrenched distribution.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Superior post-training is a real advantage, but on its own it wears off quickly. Techniques spread fast. RLHF, DPO, constitutional methods, reasoning-focused RL like o1 and DeepSeek-R1, and verifier-based training were each matched or published within months. Distillation makes it worse: a competitor can train on a leader's outputs and copy much of its behavior cheaply, and terms-of-service bans are hard to enforce. DeepSeek and others narrowed the reasoning gap far faster than the pretraining-compute gap would suggest.

What lasts is the system that produces post-training, not any single recipe. That includes proprietary preference and usage data from deployment at scale, expert-labeled data pipelines, reward models and RL environments built up over years, evaluation infrastructure, and the tacit know-how of teams that ship well-behaved models over and over. Quality in character, reliability and agentic skill comes from many small choices that are harder to copy than benchmark scores.

In short, any single post-training lead probably lasts months. A lab's ability to keep producing those leads, fed by distribution and data flywheels, can last much longer. But the real moat comes from post-training combined with compute, talent and product position, not from post-training alone.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Superior post-training is generally a short-to-medium-term advantage rather than a deeply durable standalone moat. Purely algorithmic breakthroughs—such as new reinforcement learning objectives, preference-optimization techniques, or reasoning-scaling recipes—diffuse quickly through research publications, talent mobility, and open-weight releases. Moreover, competitors can often close much of a capability gap within months by distilling outputs from a leading model or generating synthetic training data at a fraction of the original R&D cost.

Where post-training does become meaningfully more defensible is when it is anchored in assets that cannot be easily copied from model outputs alone. Proprietary, high-signal feedback flywheels from large-scale user and enterprise deployments, custom verifiable RL environments and graders for complex agentic workflows, and tightly integrated evaluation infrastructure compound over time and are difficult to replicate. Ultimately, post-training recipes themselves are perishable; durable defensibility comes from the proprietary data, environments, and product distribution that continuously feed them.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Superior post-training can create a meaningful lead, but a single breakthrough is usually a temporary moat. Recipes spread through papers and hiring, and rivals can recover some gains by training on a leading model’s outputs. DeepSeek-R1 showed how distillation could transfer substantial reasoning gains to smaller models. A rival can also erase part of the lead by starting with a stronger base model. [DeepSeek-R1 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948)

The more durable advantage is the ability to improve faster with each release. Proprietary feedback from real tasks, reliable ways to verify success on hard problems, and infrastructure that makes experiments cheap and fast can compound. Competitors can study the resulting behavior, but outputs alone reveal little about which failures to train on next or how to score them. The moat is strongest when the lab has privileged access to those signals and can keep turning them into improvements users value.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Superior post-training can give a frontier lab a meaningful lead, but a one-time breakthrough is a weak long-term moat. Rivals with comparably capable base models can learn from published methods, study product behavior, and use a leading model’s outputs to train their own. A lead on tasks with clear success criteria, such as coding problems with automated tests, can narrow quickly.

The more durable advantage is the ability to keep improving faster than competitors. A lab with exclusive access to expert feedback and real-world outcomes can discover failures that public benchmarks miss. If it can reliably turn those failures into better training data and evaluations, each deployment can inform the next model. That advantage is harder to copy because a rival can observe an answer more easily than it can observe whether the answer worked for the user. Superior post-training is therefore most defensible when it reflects a feedback loop competitors cannot readily reproduce.
